source_refs.note: Topic 18.8.1 with X-linked recessive, X-linked dominant and Y-linked traits and the SRY For Information box (PDF 106-108); Figures 18.15 to 18.17 are replaced by the original diagrams.

blocks.text: X-linked recessive traits are less common in females than in males. A female shows such a trait only when both her X chromosomes carry the recessive allele, while a male shows it with only one allele on his X, because the Y carries no allele of the gene. So the trait appears in every male who has its allele. Examples are muscular dystrophy, red-green colour-blindness and haemophilia.

items: If a mother has the trait, all her sons have it.
If a mother is a carrier (heterozygous), 50% of her sons can inherit it.
If a father has it, all his daughters are carriers, because they receive his X, and no son inherits it, because sons do not receive his X.

blocks.alt: Person icons. A carrier mother XRXr and a non-carrier father XRY. Eggs Xr and XR; sperm XR and Y. Lines join them to four children: daughters XRXr (carrier) and XRXR (non-carrier); sons XrY (trait present) and XRY (non-carrier). Key: R, X-linked dominant allele; r, X-linked recessive allele.
blocks.caption: Figure 18.15: Inheritance of X-linked recessive traits (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 18.15).

blocks.text: Examples are vitamin D-resistant rickets (inability to metabolize vitamin D properly, which softens and weakens the bones), Rett syndrome (a neuro-developmental disorder with loss of speech, repetitive hand movements and problems with walking) and Aicardi syndrome (abnormal development of the brain).

items: If the mother has the trait (homozygous or heterozygous), 50% of her children can inherit it.
If the father has it, all his daughters inherit it and no son does.

blocks.title: In both sexes
blocks.text: X-linked dominant traits are more common in females than in males.

blocks.alt: Person icons. A mother with the trait XRXr and a non-carrier father XrY. Eggs XR and Xr; sperm Xr and Y. Lines join them to four children: daughters XRXr (trait present) and XrXr (non-carrier); sons XRY (trait present) and XrY (non-carrier). Key: R, X-linked dominant allele; r, X-linked recessive allele.
blocks.caption: Figure 18.16: Inheritance of X-linked dominant traits (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 18.16).

blocks.text: The Y chromosome has relatively few genes compared with the X, so Y-linked traits are rare. Y-linked genes have no alleles on the X; they are called holandric genes and lie only on the non-homologous region of the Y. Y-linked traits appear only in males and pass from father to son only. Examples are hypertrichosis (hair on the rim of the pinna), 'porcupine man' (straight hair on the body) and webbing of the toes.

blocks.alt: Person icons. A non-carrier mother XX and a father with the trait XYr. Eggs X and X; sperm X and Yr. Lines join them to four children: two daughters XX (non-carriers) and two sons XYr (trait present). Key: r, Y-linked allele.
blocks.caption: Figure 18.17: Inheritance of Y-linked traits (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 18.17).

blocks.title: For information: the SRY gene
blocks.text: Human males have a specific gene on the Y chromosome called SRY (sex-determining region Y). It makes a protein that starts the development of the testes and prevents the development of female reproductive structures.
